newsitem.title: USA: U.S. yield curve seen steepening with Fed on hold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. yield curve seen steepening with Fed on hold.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury yield curve is likely to steepen as the short end of the market adjusts to the Federal Reserve's decision to keep monetary policy unchanged, analysts said on Tuesday.

Analysts said the spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond may widen to around 100 points over the next few days from an average of 79 points registered in the week preceding the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
Shortly after the Fed announced its decision to leave rates unchanged, the spread between the two securities was 85 basis points.

"The curve steepened a little bit, which is what you would expect ... I think there is a little more room for (further) steepening," said Leonard Santow, managing director at consulting firm Griggs & Santow Inc.

Analysts said, however, the possible drop in short-term yields is limited. "The two-year (yield) can probably get down to 6.0 percent, but at that level I think there would be total lack of interest," Santow said.
Experts said returns below 6.0 percent on the two-year will not be attractive taking into account that the federal funds rate remains steady at 5.25 percent.
Shortly after the announcement of the Fed decision, the two-year note was up 6/32 at 99-31/32 to yield 6.14 percent. The benchmark 30-year bond was up 11/32 at 96-30/32, yielding 6.99 percent.
At the long end of the curve, analysts said the scope for lower yields is also restricted.

They said that although upward pressure from wages and items other than food and energy have not yet shown through to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), inflationary fears have not been totally wiped out.

"Currently, the pipeline pressures seem quite muted. We're seeing some reports of scattered wage pressures, but they haven't really fomented into increases at the finished good levels," said Kathy Bostjancic, economist at UBS Securities.
"Going forward, however, if wage pressures grow and the companies are able to pass on some of the wage increases, then indeed you can see an uptick on inflation," she added.

But the final answer to that question will depend on the performance of the economy's fundamentals. Analysts said a new batch of key economic data to be released over the next couple of weeks will provide the market's first insight.
Crucial September figures will be released over the next 15 days, including the National Association of Purchasing Management index on October 1 and the employment report on October 4.
So far, the consensus appears to be leaning toward the notion that upcoming indicators will show an economy that is losing steam.
"We are looking for numbers coming on the weak side," Bostjancic said.
President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday that he thought the Fed's decision to leave interest rates unchanged showed the economy was strong with no signs of inflation.
"I just think it shows we've got a strong economy with no inflation. I'm glad about that," Clinton said.
Some analysts, however, said warning signs continue to flash, adding that talk of a possible rate hike at the next policy gathering on November 13 is not far-fetched.

"The economy is slowing down, but I think it's still growing above its potential ... We're seeing early warning signs that inflation is beginning to stir," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"I can see the bearish case (for the bond market) for the longer-term," he added.
The Daiwa chief economist said he expects overall consumer prices to rise by 3.3 percent in 1996, against 2.8 percent registered last year.
Moran also predicted that core CPI -- which excludes food and energy -- will stay at 3.0 percent this year, unchanged from the previous year.
